items.title: British women got the vote in two instalments: 1918 and 1928
items.claim: When did UK women win equal voting rights with men?

options.text: 1918 — full equal franchise immediately after WWI
1918 gave the vote to women over 30 meeting property qualifications (around 8.4 million); 1928 (Equal Franchise Act) gave it to all women over 21 on the same terms as men

items.reveal:
The Representation of the People Act 1918 enfranchised women over 30 who were householders, married to householders, occupiers of property at £5+ rent or university graduates. Men got the vote at 21 (or 19 if a serviceman).

The WSPU (Pankhursts, 1903), the NUWSS (Millicent Fawcett, constitutionalist) and women's war work all contributed. The 1918 compromise was partly designed to keep women a minority of the electorate.

The Equal Franchise Act 1928 gave women the vote at 21 on the same terms as men. Emmeline Pankhurst died on 14 June 1928, weeks before it took effect.
items.why: Reform is rarely complete in one step. The 10-year gap between 1918 and 1928 is itself part of the history — a partial victory deliberately designed to limit female political weight.

items.title: The Great Reform Act 1832 added only about 200,000 voters
items.claim: How dramatic was the 1832 Reform Act's franchise extension?

options.text: It increased the electorate from around 400,000 to around 650,000 (roughly 1 in 7 adult males), redistributed seats from 'rotten boroughs' to industrial cities, and explicitly excluded women
It removed all voting restrictions for property

items.reveal:
Old Sarum (one of the most notorious rotten boroughs) had no inhabitants but returned two MPs. Manchester, Birmingham and Leeds had none. The 1832 Act abolished 56 small boroughs and gave seats to industrial centres.

The £10 householder franchise in boroughs admitted urban middle-class voters; the 40-shilling freeholder in counties remained. Women were explicitly excluded for the first time (previously they had been excluded by custom).

The Second Reform Act (1867, Disraeli) added urban working-class men; the Third (1884, Gladstone) extended this to county householders. Adult male suffrage came only in 1918.
items.why: 'Great' reform was incremental. The 1832 Act is correctly remembered as a turning point — but as a beginning, not a conclusion. The disappointment fuelled Chartism (1838-1858) and the long campaign that followed.
